source: Graphs of Simple Harmonic Motion
Position, velocity and acceleration follow sine and cosine curves, each a quarter cycle apart.
Students think position and velocity reach their peaks at the same moment.

The reference circle gave the period of simple harmonic motion. It also gives the whole motion as a graph, and you can read velocity and acceleration from it just as you did with motion graphs along a line.

Follow a point around a circle of radius $A$ at angular speed $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, starting at $x = A$. Its shadow is at $x = A\cos(\omega t)$. The point's velocity has size $A\omega$ along the circle, and the shadow gets the $x$-part of it: $v = -A\omega\sin(\omega t)$. Its acceleration has size $A\omega^2$ toward the center, and the shadow's part is $a = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 x$. Cosine and sine are the same wave shifted by a quarter turn, so the three graphs are a quarter cycle apart.

Starting from $x = A$ at rest: $$x = A\cos\frac{2\pi t}{T}, \quad v = -\frac{2\pi A}{T}\sin\frac{2\pi t}{T}, \quad a = -\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 x.$$ The greatest speed is $v_{\max} = \dfrac{2\pi A}{T}$ and the greatest acceleration is $a_{\max} = \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 A$. Velocity peaks a quarter cycle after position; acceleration is always opposite to position.
Position, velocity and acceleration, each a quarter cycle from the next.
One cycle of $x = A\cos(2\pi t/T)$, a quarter at a time.
Worked examples
An $x$–$t$ graph of a mass on a spring has peaks at $x = 0.20\ \text{m}$, at $t = 0$ and $t = 2.0\ \text{s}$. Find $A$, $T$ and the greatest speed.
Reading a graph
Amplitude: from the middle line to a peak, $A = 0.20\ \text{m}$.
Period: peak to peak, $T = 2.0\ \text{s}$.
$v_{\max} = \dfrac{2\pi A}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi(0.20)}{2.0} = 0.63\ \text{m/s}$, when the graph crosses $x = 0$.
For that motion, where is the mass at $t = 0.30\ \text{s}$?
Position at a given time
The angle is in radians: $\dfrac{2\pi(0.30)}{2.0} = 0.94\ \text{rad}$.
The slope of the $x$–$t$ graph is the velocity.

Thinking position and velocity reach their peaks at the same moment. When $x$ is at its peak the mass is at a turning point, momentarily at rest: the graph is flat there, so $v = 0$. The velocity is largest a quarter cycle later, where the $x$–$t$ graph crosses zero at its steepest. Check by slopes: a peak of $x$ always lines up with a zero of $v$.
